entry.title: Congratulations, Dr. Chiu!
entry.content:
Yesterday, Alvin Chiu passed his Ph.D. defense. Alvin has been a student of Mike Goodrich at UC Irvine, is one of my coauthors, and is currently my teaching assistant for my computational geometry course.

He came to UCI from Georgia Tech, where he already had an undergraduate research paper on counting the number of ways an origami pattern can be folded, with William Hoganson, Tom Hull, and Sylvia Wu: “Counting locally flat-foldable origami configurations via 3-coloring graphs” [arXiv:1910.01278; Graphs and Combinatorics 2020, doi:10.1007/s00373-020-02240-2].

Alvin’s dissertation, Witness Drawings in Structure and Geography for Graph Visualization, is on graph drawing, with a more practical focus than my own usual theoretical approach. It takes as its motivating theme the idea that graph drawings should not merely faithfully represent a given graph (different graphs should have different drawings) and allow users to find the information they need in it, but they should also represent important graph properties or data, such as planarity, in a way that allows both for efficient checks of these properties and for readers to be able to clearly see that the property is valid. For example, drawings of planar graphs should be non-crossing (demonstrating that the graph is planar) but more than this, they should be sufficiently uncluttered that readers can clearly tell that they are planar.

I’ve already written here about two of the three publications that went into Alvin’s dissertation: “Manipulating weights to improve stress-graph drawings of 3-connected planar graphs” (from Graph Drawing 2023) and “Visualizing treewidth” (from Graph Drawing 2025). So rather than repeating that material, I thought it would make sense here to say more about the third of these publications, “Circle quasi-cartograms: Dorling cartograms with edge connections and relaxed overlap conditions” [with Tarlan Bahadori, Ahmed Eldawy, and Mike Goodrich, GeoHCC 2025, doi:10.1145/3764917.3771335].

The basic idea here is that of a cartogram, a distorted map of a geographic region where the areas of each subregion represent some kind of statistical datum about the subregion rather than its physical shape and size. A Dorling cartogram represents each subregion as a circular disk of the appropriate area, not overlapping any of the other disks. There is a free parameter, the scale of these disks; if they are all scaled to be very small, they can be placed at their correct geographic positions, but this small scale causes the information in the cartogram to be difficult to discern. On the other hand, if the scale is increased, the disks cannot all fit in their correct geographic locations; the cartogram necessarily distorts both geographic position, and, more subtly, the topological connections between the disks. For instance, if we draw a graph of the adjacencies between bordering subregions, then it will for the most part be planar for a geographic placement of vertices at the center of each region, but the distortions caused by a larger cartogram scale can lead to nonplanarities.

Alvin’s paper on cartograms tries to ameliorate these problems with Dorling cartograms by relaxing their hard non-overlap constraints. Instead, he uses a force-based graph drawing system in which the vertices move to minimize an energy resulting from the combination of three forces: attractions between the vertices and their correct geographic locations, and between pairs of neighboring vertices, but repulsions between vertices whose circles overlap, depending on the degree of overlap. These are controlled by three parameters that set the scale of the circles and the relative strengths of these three forces. Their results are tested experimentally, showing that even when a cartogram with no overlap is desired as the eventual result, this method can significantly reduce the mixing of vertices from distinct regions, while paying for this by introducing smaller-scale edge crossings.

Congratulations, Alvin!

(Discuss on Mastodon)

entry.title: Linkage
entry.content:
• How Wikipedia’s editors (try to) keep the online encyclopedia human-written (\(\mathbb{M}\), via). Eliza Strickland of IEEE Spectrum interviews Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of Wikipedia’s AI Cleanup project.

  • Analyzing the simplex method by-the-book (\(\mathbb{M}\)). 21-minute STOC’26 video by Sophie Huiberts and her collaborators, explaining why the rounding and random perturbations commonly used in implementations of the simplex method for linear programming make it behave differently from worst-case exponential examples, converging in polynomial time to good solutions for well-scaled input instances. See also their STOC paper.

  • I’m pretty sure I’ve complained about this before (\(\mathbb{M}\)), but when my campus’s photographer (officially a managing producer-director in the Office of Strategic Communications & Public Affairs) comes around to take free faculty/staff portraits, as he does every couple of years, he tells us “you can do what you want with them”, but it’s not true. It’s a work for hire, so the copyright on the photos is owned by the Regents of the University of California, who will not release them under an open-access Creative Commons license, so they cannot be used for instance on Wikipedia. Nobody has figured out the cheat codes for this piece of bureaucracy, so we end up getting a nice set of photos that are not actually as usable as they should be.

    Anyway, I have a new headshot. I kind of like how it came out, but the best my family will say about it is “it looks like you”. To spare you all from having to look at my no-longer-middle-aged face, I won’t inline it here, but you can find a copy on my home page.

  • A dot planimeter (\(\mathbb{M}\)) is just a fancy name for a transparent sheet with a square grid of dots printed onto it. You can estimate the areas of shapes by overlaying it on the shape and counting the dots. Now another Good Article on Wikipedia.

  • University libraries are being swarmed by AI bots, putting public access at risk (\(\mathbb{M}\)), says the CBC.

  • Richard Schwartz discovers how to fold the simplest origami torus (\(\mathbb{M}\)). Manon Bischoff in Scientific American; see also Schwartz’s PNAS paper.

  • I upgraded my phone today (\(\mathbb{M}\)), at an office of my service provider, a couple miles from my house. As I was finishing up the purchase, the sales clerk asked me a question so unexpected that I had to stop for a few seconds to figure out what she meant: Do you know how to get home?

    The point was that my phone wouldn’t be able to map the way for me until I had set it up. I almost never use in-car maps; if it’s not a place I’ve been before, I’d much prefer to study a map beforehand and memorize the route, and if (as in this case) I’ve been there before I can remember it. But so many people today have lost that skill and in many cases can’t even read a map. I find it all a bit sad.

    So yes, I did know how to get home.

  • I made this illustration (\(\mathbb{M}\)) for the Wikipedia article on the problem of folding a square to make a shape of greater perimeter than you started with. It depicts a map from a square to a tree, that does not increase any distance (a “short map”), but that does increase the perimeter of its image. Each red circle or blue circular arc in the square is mapped to its thick centerline at the point where it crosses the centerline; these centerlines become the branches of the tree. The yellow regions of the square are all mapped to a single point where the branches meet. The perimeter of the black part of the tree is the same as the square; the doubled length of the red branch is added on top of that. Svetlana Krat’s 2005 Ph.D. thesis includes both this map (and its generalization to rectangles) and a method of approximating short maps by foldings, to give a novel solution to the napkin folding problem.

  • Why are rivers so mathematical? (\(\mathbb{M}\)). Natalie Wolchover in Quanta on the scaling laws of river networks.

  • Knotting spheres in the 4th dimension (\(\mathbb{M}\)). 4-minute video by Henry Segerman that combines 3d printing with the 2d drawing conventions of 1d knots in 3d, to make 3d knot diagrams of 2d knots in 4d.

  • On the statistics of close multiway elections (\(\mathbb{M}\)), using the recent Mississippi US Senate race as an example.

  • All 1665 submissions to STOC 2027, online (\(\mathbb{M}\)) following STOC’s new procedure of publication first, verdict afterwards.

  • Catherine Holloway explains her uncle David Huffman’s work on the mathematics of origami (\(\mathbb{M}\)). 21-minute YouTube talk.

  • Inscribed zonotopes, simplicial arrangements, and reflection groups (\(\mathbb{M}\)), Sebastian Manecke and Raman Sanyal. These are an unusual class of special zonotopes all of whose vertices belong to a sphere, in 17 combinatorial types, several of which are animated in the Mastodon thread. The planar equivalent, zonotopal tilings in which all faces are inscribed in circles, turn out to be dual to simplicial arrangements.

entry.title: MathML-mania cripples Wikipedia mathematics, again
entry.content:
Last week, the Wikimedia developers switched mathematics rendering on the English-language Wikipedia to a new system, so badly broken that it cannot correctly render the inequivalence relation symbol \(\not\equiv\), with formulas often partially obscured by other content such as images preventing them from being viewed, and intermittently not showing some formulas in footnote mouseovers at all. The changeover does not appear to have fixed old and long-unfixed bugs such as the inability to use mathematical formulas in image captions (if you do, clicking on the image will give you an expanded view with a broken caption). They did this without any large scale testing, without the ability for individuals to use their viewing preferences to restore the old system, with essentially no consultation with the mathematics editors on Wikipedia, without advance notice to Wikipedia, and over the repeated strong objections of the mathematics editors who despite all this found out ahead of time that this change was imminent. How did we get here?

When Knuth developed TeX in the late 1970s, it combined a shorthand textual notation for mathematical formulas that already by that time had become commonplace in networked email conversations between mathematicians, with Knuth’s obsessive care and attention to the fine details of mathematical typography. Others extended TeX in the early 1980s, producing AMS-TeX and LaTeX, which became and remain the standard for all professional mathematics. The relative ease of creating formulas in text, and the high-quality results, were never replicated by the word processors and point-and-click equation editors of the later 1980s. But this was all aimed at creating paginated mathematical documents, so when Wikipedia was founded in 2001 the web was in something of a mathematical dark age. You could write formulas as text, or you could use LaTeX on the server side to create a bitmap image file displaying the formula. It would be pixelated, with likely the wrong font size and alignment, but at least it would match the carefully developed formula layout that Knuth had designed. That was what Wikipedia chose, and it was the right choice at the time. Wikipedia editors could write formulas formatted as TeX, and the results would be far from beautiful, but at least they would be sort of legible.

MathJax became available in 2009, and quickly changed all that. One could write mathematical formulas as LaTeX formulas in the source code of web pages, and a JavaScript library in your browser would convert the formulas into something very close to Knuth’s layout, but formatted as text rather than as an image (so it would be affected by other text formatting like the coloring of links to other sites), in a font closely matching the one used for the rest of the web page’s text. MathJax quickly caught on, both for big sites (like MathSciNet, a database of reviews of mathematics publication) and small ones like personal blogs, and continues to be used with some competition from KaTeX, a similar JavaScript library. Early versions of MathJax were slow to render and worked best with big local font library installations but both of these issues were subsequently much improved.

There were desultory efforts to incorporate MathJax into Wikipedia, never fully supported, but by 2015, they had been ripped out again and Wikipedia’s mathematics formatting was still server-side images only. That remained true until last week, although the images gradually became higher-quality vector graphics, and closer to the body font in size and alignment, as this method was polished over time. The situation was already so frustrating to me in 2015 that I wrote a long blog post about it, “MathML considered harmful”. As the title suggests, I blamed MathML for the failure of Wikimedia’s developers to provide Wikipedia with MathJax, or with anything resembling MathJax in its combination of ease of use by Wikipedia editors and high quality output presented to viewers. The developers of Wikipedia’s formula-presentation software had focused all their attention on MathML, a dead end, at the expense of improving its image-based rendering system, and appeared to have been intentionally blocking the use of MathJax because they saw it as a competitor to their favored system, MathML.

MathML is an XML-based format for encoding mathematics formulas, first released in the late 1990s when XML was being used for everything. That has since changed; the standards bodies that control html have backtracked on XML compatibility, and JSON has taken over much of the data formatting that had been done with XML. One XML format that is unproblematic and remains in wide use is SVG, a vector graphics format; it is the preferred format for uploading technical illustrations to Wikipedia (although the servers convert them to bitmaps before presenting them to readers) and was the image format presented to readers for mathematics formulas in Wikipedia before the recent changes. However, MathML has been much less successful than SVG. It is neither easy to edit by hand (unlike TeX-based formats) nor easy for browsers to render well (maybe in part because there is little commercial pressure for them to do so). By 2013, MathML had become so disused that Google removed MathML support from its Chrome browser, and the only plugin available for Internet Explorer stopped working. And as of my 2015 post, the MathML designers had fallen back on a dual language design: one variant of MathML for semantics, an entirely different variant for formatting, with marketing that cherry-picked the supposed benefits of each variant as if they were all the same thing. But because the MathML designers neither tried to mimic TeX nor had Knuth’s focus on producing mathematical typography, the formatting version of MathML adequately described the rough layout of a formula but did not lend itself well to high-quality typography. And the dream of a semantically meaningful XML-based interchange language for mathematics was always a dream: when used as a natural language for communicating mathematics between humans, there are too many ambiguities and abuses of notation for a mechanical formalization to work.

It seems the developers never stopped dreaming. A 2023 web page from the Daisy Consortium (which develops MathML) proclaims “Now that MathML is natively supported in Safari, Firefox, Chrome, and Edge, websites and publishers can confidently use MathML for math expressions, with the benefits this brings for accessibility”. There are no benefits for accessibility: TeX, based as it is on textual email shorthands, is much better than MathML for screen readers. And side-by-side comparisons of LaTeX versus browser renderings of MathML reveal that, still today, the MathML rendering does not achieve the same high quality as TeX. But as recently as 2024, the Wikimedia developers were prepared to replace all mathematics rendering on Wikipedia with MathML: TeX formulas in the Wikipedia source code would be converted on the server side to MathML, and sent to readers whose browsers would render and display the MathML as something. When the plan was discovered, Wikipedia’s mathematics editors raised an outcry over the resulting degradation in typographic quality, and the developers backed off.

Nevertheless, the old server-side image-based rendering needed to be replaced, because the image caching database that it was based on had become unmaintainable. And the 2024 debacle meant that direct MathML would not work. So this brought us to a new plan and last week’s update. The new rendering system is called “client-side SVG”. But what that really means is: the server converts the TeX source code from Wikipedia to MathML, and sends it to browsers, just like the developers always wanted to do. But because the browsers do not render MathML well, there’s one more step: on the browser side, they use MathJax to convert the MathML back into a rendered formula.

MathJax does use MathML as an internal format for its formulas, so this is not complete nonsense, but needless to say, this is not how MathJax is intended to be used. It should not be surprising that translating mathematics formulas from TeX into what is essentially a foreign language and back before rendering them has some problems. The surprise is, instead, that it works at all. But there are many bugs, the system is inevitably fragile and unlikely to survive any updates to MathJax, and the fact that the Wikimedia side of the conversion is being handled by a small project with very few developers makes triaging and fixing any bugs very slow.

As for the broken inequivalence symbol bug: it’s at the cosmetic level, an ugly rendering but one that can still be read. Instead of \(\not\equiv\), it is displayed with the slash off-center, farther to the right than it should be. It’s the sort of thing that distracts and slows down readers, but doesn’t really prevent them from understanding the intended meaning. So it may be a long time before it is fixed. But I think it makes a good test case for the overblown claims that MathML makes formulas more accessible, more readable, and render well. In TeX, in MathJax-based systems (such as this blog), and in Wikipedia’s content editor, one codes this symbol by \not\equiv. The backslashes mark the beginning of the name of something, the first \not puts a slash through the next thing, and the next thing is the name of equivalence relation symbol. If a screenreader spoke “not equiv” I think it would be clear enough. On my blog, you should be able to control-click or left-click on the rendered symbol at the start of this paragraph and reach an accessibility menu that includes text-to-speech options. But in MathML, as currently coded by Wikipedia from this input, and indented for greater readability, it becomes:

So readable! So accessible! So semantic! The meaningful part is hidden in the inner line (the one with the most indentation): the two characters ≡ (the equivalence symbol) and ̸ (the unicode “combining long solidus overlay” symbol). When placed together in text they would normally appear one after the other but somehow the client-side rendering library knows to overlay them and does so, but fails to center them vertically. In this example it would be possible to combine them into a single unicode inequivalence symbol, ≢, but I wouldn’t want them to try to patch this bug by trying to convert to it, because then the bug would still be present for all the more-obscure symbols that didn’t get the same treatment. And on Wikipedia, as well as rendering badly, there is no accessibility menu, and the image displaying the badly-rendered inequivalence symbol appears not to have any alt text. There’s an “Explain mathematical formulae on hover” option in Wikipedia’s viewing preferences, for logged-in users, but it appears to do nothing in my browser. So the only choice for accessibility seems to be to set one’s preferences to display the TeX source code directly rather than doing anything to render a formula.

In the absence of visible effort from the developers to catalog and prioritize the many bugs in this new rendering system, some Wikipedia editors have made their own catalog: Wikipedia:WikiProject Mathematics/MathFormattingBugs. It is a few months old, created when (despite no communication from Wikimedia) the editors caught wind of the plans to implement the new system, and hoped to either head it off (unsuccessfully) or at least delay its launch until the system worked reliably (also unsuccessfully). It at least had the effect of triggering the fixes of other bugs that were even more severe than the ones still listed, that otherwise likely would still not be fixed. But this bug catalog, too, was broken by the changeover to the new rendering system. It previously showed, for each example of a buggy formula, a side-by-side comparison of the old rendering system (“server-side SVG”), the new rendering (“client-side SVG”), and the rendering you would get by passing the MathML directly to your browser. This comparison is no longer available, because the developers ripped out the old rendering system at the same time that they made the new system the default.

(Discuss on Mastodon)

entry.title: Linkage for a rainy Halloween
entry.content:
• Elliot Kienzle illustrates the AI proof of the Mahler conjecture (\(\mathbb{M}\)) on symplectic embeddings of a ball into the Cartesian product of a convex body and its dual, showing that the product’s volume is always at least as large as the ball.

  • On the generation of names of weevils and popes by L-systems (\(\mathbb{M}\)).

  • Marginalia search (\(\mathbb{M}\)), a web search engine that prioritizes the stuff the big ones don’t: text-heavy, non-commercial pages, personal blogs, old university pages, and the like.

  • Sudoku but you have to prove your answer before it’s allowed. Which raises the question: prove under what assumptions? Are you allowed to assume uniqueness in your proofs?

  • Borromean hexagonal tilings, embedded orthogonally in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) in such a way that removing one of them allows the other two to be pulled apart.

  • Lance Fortnow on reading messy proofs (\(\mathbb{M}\)). He quotes Noam Nisan as saying that “reading a badly written proof leads to better understanding since you really need to figure out the details”.

  • Mathematics Genealogy Project temporarily offline (\(\mathbb{M}\)) because of the recently-discovered security vulnerabilities in PHP. Unfortunately their software was incompatible with recent versions so it wasn’t a matter of a simple upgrade. They’re asking for donations to cover both a backend overhaul (estimated to cost more than half their typical annual budget) and catching up on their severe backlog of updates (almost a year deep).

  • The Perles configuration of nine points and nine lines (\(\mathbb{M}\)) is based on a regular pentagon/pentagram; it cannot be realized by points with rational-number Cartesian coordinates, even in less-symmetrical arrangements of its points and lines. But there are stronger ways to be difficult to realize than irrationality. We can’t hope for transcendentality: when a configuration can be realized it can always be realized using algebraic number coordinates. An intermediate step between these two is unconstructibility: can it be drawn with compass and straightedge? Because the Perles configuration is based on a regular pentagon, it is obviously constructible.

    The Grünbaum–Rigby configuration is based in a similar way on regular heptagons/heptagrams. Because these cannot be constructed with compass and straightedge, neither can the symmetric form of the Grünbaum–Rigby configuration. I suspect the same is true for any asymmetric forms it might have but I have no proof. (I did try asking a couple of advanced-model LLMs; one told me it had no idea and another told me it was unconstructible but retreated when pressed for details.) One property of the Perles configuration that helps prove its irrationality is projective uniqueness: any two realizations are related by a projective transformation, together with a permutation of the points and lines of the configuration. If this were true of the Grünbaum–Rigby configuration it would prove unconstructibility but I don’t know whether it’s true.

  • 3d-printed tiles from the aperiodic chair tiling snap together like Lego (\(\mathbb{M}\)) in this short (2:18) video by Bob Mackay explaining its recursive structure.

  • LLMs still can’t count. A story about trying to count the teeth on a bicycle sprocket wheel, getting an answer that isn’t a valid tooth count, asking the LLM to label the teeth on a photo, and getting back a replacement photo with more teeth that still aren’t even counted correctly.

  • OEIS A400K contest winners (\(\mathbb{M}\)). The top entry: A400000, the “city-building sequence” in which \(a(n)\) is the height \(h\) of the shortest building which can see exactly \(h\) earlier buildings of heights \(a(i)\), in an unobstructed line of site from its roof.

  • I updated the talk slides for my talk “Computational complexities of folding” (\(\mathbb{M}\)), on connections between computational complexity theory and origami, for a presentation to a local student group. The updates included a last-minute change to a slide on the exponential time hypothesis to take into account the OpenAI claimed disproof, but their result doesn’t really change things for what I was using it for: if the exponential part of a time bound has an exponent that is linear in a certain parameter (as pre-disproof ETH would imply), or near-linear in it (consistent with the disproof), it’s still a big time bound. Since I originally presented this material in 2024 I’ve published a journal version detailing much of the talk; see also my publication metadata page.

  • The lattice of stable matchings (\(\mathbb{M}\)) organizes the set of all solutions of a stable matching problem into a structure in which each two matchings have a least upper bound (giving all the participants on one side their preference among the two partners from the two matchings) and a greatest lower bound (the same for the participants on the other side). Its uses involve algorithms for finding weight-maximizing or regret-minimizing stable matchings. A little technical still, but now a Good Article on Wikipedia.

  • Why Richard Elwes loves Stella (\(\mathbb{M}\)), software for constructing and visualizing polyhedra.

  • How inappropriate it is for referees/editors to use AI to help review any original work. A computer can never be held accountable for breaching the confidentiality of submissions; therefore, a computer must never be given access to confidential submissions.

entry.title: Congratulations, Dr. Liu!
entry.content:
Another UC Irvine doctoral student, Songyu (Alfred) Liu, successfully passed his doctoral defense this week, co-advised by Mike Goodrich and me.

Alfred came to UCI in 2020, initially working with cognitive scientist Mark Steyvers, who has a joint appointment in computer science. Their work eventually turned into a 2024 publication, “Combining Human and AI Strengths in Object Counting under Information Asymmetry”, in the 12th AAAI Conference on Human Computation and Crowdsourcing (2024), but in the meantime Alfred decided that he preferred topics that were more directly computational, and switched to working with Mike Goodrich (and eventually me).

The three topics of his doctoral dissertation are reconstructing graphs from shortest path queries (the sort of information you might obtain from the Unix ping command), connections between different graph width parameters, and graph drawing, and are represented in an overlapping way by the three publications that Alfred combined to form his thesis:

  • “Exact learning of weighted graphs using composite queries” (with Goodrich and Ioannis Panageas, IWOCA 2025, arXiv:2511.14882), concerns reconstruction using weighted shortest path and distance queries, generalizing previous results on unweighted graphs. The main result is that for a given connected graph with bounded degree and \(n\) vertices, with edge weights drawn from a power-law distribution, the graph can be reconstructed with \(O(n^{3/2})\) queries, matching what was known for unweighted graphs.

  • I’ve written here before about “Bandwidth vs BFS width in matrix reordering, graph reconstruction, and graph drawing” (with Goodrich and me, ESA 2025, arXiv:2505.10789), which I think is the strongest of the three papers. It shows that a simple and widely used breadth-first search based approximation to graph bandwidth, the Cuthill–McKee algorithm, provides a polylogarithmic approximation to bounded bandwidth, with an exponent in the polylogarithm that depends on the bandwidth, and that this dependence is necessary. Applications include reconstruction of bounded-bandwidth graphs in a near-linear number of queries, and drawing graphs as arc diagrams using arcs of small height.

    Some later work by others on similar problems is also worth mentioning here. “Cutwidth versus BFS-width with applications to graph reconstruction from distance queries” (Chirag Kaudan and Amir Nayyeri, SWAT 2026), shows that the same BFS-based heuristic approximates a stronger graph width parameter, cutwidth, with an approximation ratio that is sublinear for bounded cutwidth, with an exponent that depends on the cutwidth. And “Forbidden subgraphs of graphs with low bandwidth” (Maria Chudnovsky, Daniel Lokshtanov, and Eran Nevo, STOC 2026, arXiv:2609.01949) provides a significantly more accurate (but likely less practical) approximation to bandwidth, with an approximation ratio that is bounded rather than polylogarithmic for bounded bandwidth.

  • “Layer-respecting linear graph layouts” (by Alvin Chiu, me, Goodrich, and Alfred, CCCG 2026, arXiv:2607.06968) starts with a graph that has already been partitioned into layers, such as would be obtained by using BFS to approximate bandwidth or cutwidth. For several variations on graph drawing styles that draw the vertices in separate layers or in a single linear sequence with each layer contiguous, we use dynamic programming to optimally order the vertices within each layer in order to minimize the number of crossings in the drawing.

Congratulations, Alfred!

(Discuss on Mastodon)

entry.title: Linkage
entry.content:
• arXiv imposes a new limit of two submissions per submitter per month (\(\mathbb{M}\)).

  • Book of Shapes: A collection of minimal, generative and customizable SVG-patterns (\(\mathbb{M}\), via).

  • Sham scientific societies are misleading star researchers, according to Nature (\(\mathbb{M}\), via).

  • The \(13\times 13\) zebra graph is untraceable (\(\mathbb{M}\)). A zebra is a fairy chess piece that jumps like a longer knight, two steps in one direction and three in another. Almost a proof without words that the graph of its moves on a \(13\times 13\) chessboard has no Hamiltonian path.

  • The Harvard/Smithsonian Astrophysics Data System, a large bibliographic database for astronomy, astrophysics, and related fields, has been transitioning for the last year or so to become SciX with expanded areas of coverage “across space, Earth, and planetary sciences”, and is scheduled to complete the move in mid-November (\(\mathbb{M}\)). It’s difficult to find much about the move from adsabs to SciX that isn’t both heavy on promotion and light on content, but their press release is better than some, and there’s documentation on how to use SciX.

    If you’ve ever wondered what those “bibcode” tags associated with some scientific references are, they’re pointers into this database. I imagine non-mathematicians have similar questions about what those “MR” and “Zbl” tags used for mathematical references are; the answer is the same, pointers to the MathSciNet and zbMATH databases respectively. And now I’m wondering why DBLP doesn’t have its own tags for computer science references.

  • Denny Vrandečić stumbled into a rabbit hole of unsourced Wikipedia claims about the production of a Spider Man movie, and AI hallucinations and circular reasoning when he tried to search for the missing sources and the edits that added the claims. The claims were eventually reinstated with proper sourcing, through the community of human editors of Wikipedia; Vrandečić concludes that, in contrast, “the AI in this case was actively harmful”.

  • If your \(\LaTeX\) input encodes an en-dash as a double-hyphen --, TeX will allow a line break after it. If it encodes it as a unicode en-dash character –, it will not allow a line break, both in pdflatex with \usepackage[utf8]{inputenc} and lualatex without (\(\mathbb{M}\)). Additionally, with the unicode en-dashes, pdflatex and lualatex will differ in how they break the words between the dashes: pdflatex will not break and hyphenate “Koebe–Andreev–Thurston” at all, but lualatex will break it as “Koebe–An- [line break] dreev–Thurston”. With double-hyphens, both are happy to produce the much better output “Koebe– [line break] Andreev–Thurston”. So let this be a lesson not to try to be fancy in how you type your dashes in \(\LaTeX\). Just use double hyphens (or triple hyphens for em-dashes) and let \(\LaTeX\) do the conversion to dashes.

  • On searching Wikipedia for article titles containing colons, like “ST:TNG”. It will think you are looking for an article titled “TNG” in the Sotho-language Wikipedia, regardless of how you try to escape the colon. But it turns out that, for Wikipedia, colons that are actually given in titles rather than used to demark other namespaces are equivalent to spaces. So the string you want to search for is “ST TNG”.

  • Numberphile video on Connor Hill’s classification of noble polyhedra (\(\mathbb{M}\)). A noble polyhedron has all faces and all vertices symmetric to each other, but not necessarily all edges. There are two infinite families and a lot of sporadic examples, especially if you allow self-intersections. Hill won the 2026 International Science and Engineering Fair, a high school student competition, for his determination of the complete list.

  • Show that two “ice cream cones” in a regular pentagon have the same angle (\(\mathbb{M}\)). A challenge problem on the mathematics StackExchange with a pretty diagram illustrating it.

  • Spanning surfaces of the same knot that cannot be deformed into each other, even in 4d (\(\mathbb{M}\)). Research from 2022 by Kyle Hayden, Seungwon Kim, Maggie Miller, JungHwan Park, and Isaac Sundberg, reported on at the time by Quanta, and helpful in understanding Maggie Miller’s new Joy of Why podcast episode “What Does the Fourth Dimension Actually Look Like?”.

  • What even is mathematical output? (\(\mathbb{M}\)). Among thoughts on AI in mathematics, David Roberts collects a farm of expert quotes on how horribly badly written and unintelligible the recent OpenAI preprint dump has been. Their Lean proofs aren’t any better: they contain large chunks of junk code that literally do nothing.

  • The septopert, a seven-sided polyhedron that cannot fit through a hole in itself.

  • Celebrating Loday’s associahedron (\(\mathbb{M}\)), 2023 survey by Pilaud, Santos, and Ziegler. See also two more recent articles on coloring the vertices of the associahedron: “A double-logarithmic upper bound on the chromatic number of the associahedron” (Oum and Wood), and “The chromatic number of the associahedron: simple and logarithmic” (Berendsohn, Cardinal, Iacono, and Kozma).

  • One of my cats, Smoke, looks through a window in the morning light (\(\mathbb{M}\)).

entry.title: Linkage
entry.content:
• The 3D Heesch Hemiobelisk: a nonzero-Dehn-invariant hexahedron with a complete corona (\(\mathbb{M}\)).

  • The Immerman–Szelepcsényi theorem formalized in Lean as part of the LAX Lean archive (\(\mathbb{M}\)), a form of literate programming for Lean proofs that includes definitions for computational complexity theory.

  • This year’s STOC call for papers has made significant changes, in the face of an onslaught of AI-generated submissions (\(\mathbb{M}\), via). Submissions must list authors, all of whom must be human, no author can be on more than five submissions, all submissions must be posted in identical form to arXiv prior to submission, AI use is allowed but must be disclosed, AI reviewing is also allowed subject to author consent, and (perhaps the biggest change) authors must also prepare and submit a 20-30 minute explanatory video.

  • Recognizing penny graphs is \(\exists\mathbb{R}\)-complete (\(\mathbb{M}\)), new preprint by Anna Lubiw and Marcus Schaefer. These are the graphs of tangencies of interior-disjoint unit circles, or equivalently the graphs with drawings that are simultaneously planar and unit-distance. They were known to be \(\mathsf{NP}\)-hard to recognize but this result makes their complexity more precise. The results extend to other geometric graph classes including the contact graphs of balls with unrestricted radii in 3d.

  • I’ve been using syncthing between home and office for a long time (\(\mathbb{M}\)). but somehow it hadn’t occurred to me that I could also use it to sync my music library between home computer and phone. Anyway, an up-to-date syncthing-fork is on Google Play and works for this. Unfortunately a long discussion on the syncthing forum fails to clarify how trustworthy it is.

  • Barrel game/puzzle (\(\mathbb{M}\)). Open and close pipes between given barrels of liquid to equalize their water levels, with the goal of getting at least a given level of water into one of the barrels.

  • The Cartesian product of two equilateral triangles is a 4d convex polytope with nine vertices and six triangular-prism facets, sometimes called the 3–3 duoprism (\(\mathbb{M}\)). Now remove one of the vertices and take the convex hull of the rest. You should get seven facets: an irregular tetrahedron where you removed the vertex, four pyramids (with a square base but unequal sides) surrounding it, and two triangular prisms that were unchanged by the removal. This heptatope has the property that no facet is adjacent (across a polygon) with all six others, because the facets all have four or five polygons, not six. It has the fewest facets of any convex 4-polytope with this property.

  • Cursed waffle (\(\mathbb{M}\)) with waffled indentations in the pattern of the tightest-known packing of 17 squares into a square.

  • Countable graphs with finite path-width: characterisation and universality (\(\mathbb{M}\)). New preprint by Tony Huynh, Freddie Illingworth, Nikolai Karol, Florian Lehner, Chun-Hung Liu, János Pach, and David R. Wood from a MATRIX workshop on graph structure theory.

  • How many L-seams does it take to sew Mrs. Perkins’s quilt (\(\mathbb{M}\))? New OEIS sequence from a practical crafting problem.

  • Abstract patterns from a hanging lamp and a dusty screen door (\(\mathbb{M}\)).

  • Talia Ringer worries about proof assistant kernel bugs in the Lean kernel, because although past bugs have not been things one might accidentally exploit and a human would have no incentive to do so, the rise of long unreadable machine-generated Lean proofs gives us a different threat model.

  • Discrete approximations to the Borel circle squaring problem generated by selecting a small set of translation vectors between a pixelated square and a pixelated circle and then solving a perfect matching problem. Solutions with five pieces can be found by using a heuristic search to find a good set of five translation vectors; it’s unclear whether fewer is possible.

  • NFC vs NFD unicode normalization (\(\mathbb{M}\)) or why you are probably encountering incompatibilities in filename encodings of accented characters between MacOS and everything else.

  • Hanayama makes massive versions of its most iconic cast puzzles (\(\mathbb{M}\)) and can ship internationally.

entry.content:
• Brick territories experiment (\(\mathbb{M}\)). What shapes do you get when \(n\) simultaneous breakout games compete against each other for pixels?

  • Lillian Oppenheimer, 1898–1992 (\(\mathbb{M}\)), early and significant promoter of origami in the US, founder of the organization that became OrigamiUSA, mother of notable mathematicians William Kruskal, Martin David Kruskal, and Joseph Kruskal, and grandmother of computer scientist Clyde Kruskal. Now a Good Article on Wikipedia (not one that I wrote or edited; I merely reviewed it).

  • Python sets and dictionaries can have quadratic-time performance (\(\mathbb{M}\)), for adversarially-chosen data.

  • Terry Tao on what can be learned from studying problems rather than on what their solutions happen to be.

  • Ig Nobel Prize goes to a study showing that rich people are more likely than others to steal candy from children (\(\mathbb{M}\)). The recipient, Paul Piff, is a social psychologist at UC Irvine.

  • Three dimensional dominoes (\(\mathbb{M}\)), in the same sense as the three-dimensional matching problem rather than in the geometric sense one might conventionally expect.

  • Zoom now stays alive in the background and reads everything written to the Linux/X11 clipboard. As one commenter writes, “It would be interesting to know what Zoom actually does with the captured clipboard content.” It might not actually be malware.

  • Tadashi Tokieda gave a beautiful invited presentation at JCDCG\(^3\) on the mathematics of folded and crumpled paper (\(\mathbb{M}\)). In it, he complained about the various poor choices of notation people have used for the Poisson ratio (https:// en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson%27s_ratio), and proposed instead the notation \(\mathop{\rlap{\hspace{0.12em}\cdot}{\alpha}}\) (an alpha with a dot inside it, which I have coded here as \mathop{\rlap{\hspace{0.12em}\cdot}{\alpha}}). Half of the audience (the ones who spoke any French) broke out laughing but he left the joke unexplained.

  • Slides for my talk at JCDCG\(^3\), “Patterns of Tangent Spheres” (\(\mathbb{M}\)).

  • There’s so much going on at once in the LLM/mathematics world and so many people providing insightful comment on it that I’m not even going to try to add to it (\(\mathbb{M}\)). Instead, here’s a nice recent preprint where “all original results, proof strategies, and mathematical content predate the use of AI assistance” despite some AI use in cleaning up the writeup: “Forbidden subgraphs of graphs with low bandwidth”, by Maria Chudnovsky, Daniel Lokshtanov, and Eran Nevo. Given any graph \(G\), in fixed-parameter time in a parameter \(k\), they find either a subtree of bandwidth \(\ge k\) or a linear layout of bandwidth \(\le f(k)\) for some (badly exponential) function \(f\). There is additionally a structure theorem describing the high-bandwidth subtrees as having a special form (high pathwidth, or high ratio of vertices to diameter, or a “skewed Cantor comb”.

  • A topological picture book (\(\mathbb{M}\), via). 3d topological models rendered as “hand-hatched surfaces after the mid-century manner of Francis, Apéry, Hilbert–Cohn-Vossen”. The project creator adds in the via link that it was based on Aaron Hertzmann and Denis Zorin’s “Illustrating smooth surfaces”.

  • Almost linear universal point sets for planar graphs (\(\mathbb{M}\)). New arXiv preprint by Taylor Gordon. No affiliation listed, but Gordon was a student of Anna Lubiw at Waterloo, and is apparently now at OpenAI.

  • Analog Library Premium Edition™ (\(\mathbb{M}\)), nice free landing page for any doi.

  • Peter Luschny laments the now-rapid death of most external links from OEIS.

entry.title: Periodic coloring of infinite planar graphs

link.title: Periodic coloring of infinite planar graphs

entry.content:
The de Bruijn–Erdős theorem states that the number of colors needed to color an infinite graph is the same as the maximum number needed for its finite subgraphs. So for any reasonable definition of an infinite planar graph, the 4-color theorem for finite planar graphs implies that every infinite planar graph is also 4-colorable.

One way to construct infinite planar graphs is to make them periodic: start with any periodic tiling of the plane, decorate a single prototile by vertices and edges that may wrap from one tile to the next, and form an infinite graph from the copies of these decorations on all the tiles of the tiling. One possibility is to simply use one vertex in each tile, with edges that connect that vertex to its copies in each adjacent tile, in which case coloring the graph is the same as coloring the tiles of the tiling. For instance, here are two periodic colorings of the floret pentagonal tiling, one with the same translational symmetries as the whole tiling and six colors, and a second one that repeats with a fundamental domain that is 3x as large, but with only three colors.

However, the colorings given by the de Bruijn–Erdős theorem might not be periodic at all, even for a periodic graph generated in this way. And it might not always be possible to find a 4-coloring with the same period as the embedding: that would be the same as torus graph coloring, which can sometimes need as many as 7 colors, and the 6-coloring of the floret pentagonal tiling above is optimal for that period. However, thanks to a recent preprint and a 2020 MathOverflow posting with a 2025 answer both by user “Nate” we can now prove that periodic infinite planar graphs have periodic 4-colorings.

The preprint in question is “Three-edge-coloring (Tait coloring) cubic graphs on the torus: A proof of Grünbaum’s conjecture” by Yuta Inoue, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Atsuyuki Miyashita, Bojan Mohar, and Tomohiro Sonobe, arXiv:2505.07002. Its characterization of cubic torus graphs without a 3-edge-coloring implies that every periodic planar cubic graph has a periodic 3-edge-coloring that at most doubles the fundamental domain. For finite planar graphs, cubic edge 3-coloring and vertex 4-coloring are equivalent, but in the periodic case there is another expansion by 2x in both lattice directions to go from edge coloring to 4-coloring. So the result ends up being that periodic planar graphs have 4-colorings with a fundamental domain (for their translational symmetries) that is at most 8x larger than that of the given graph.

This answers a question I asked on my blog 20 years ago (from which I copied the figure above). As I posted a few years later, periodic and aperiodic 3-coloring of periodic planar graphs can be different: there exist periodic infinite planar graphs that are 3-colorable, but for which all 3-colorings are aperiodic. The MathOverflow post on this was found by my student Cole Groen; thanks, Cole!

(Discuss on Mastodon)

entry.title: Linkage with two research problems
entry.content:
In case you’ve been worrying that the recent publicity blitz of LLM solutions to open mathematics problems is causing us to run short, there are two more mixed in among my usual links here. Because I haven’t solved them, they are not very precisely formulated, and I don’t know how difficult or interesting they are nor even whether someone else might have already considered them; that’s often the way at the start of research.

  • I think maybe I need to start bringing my DSLR along again when I go to the beach (\(\mathbb{M}\)) rather than relying on my cell phone camera (Pixel 6 Pro, yes I know it’s getting old now). Here’s what it thinks a crashing wave looks like, without additional processing except for a bit of a crop. To me it more resembles the kind of molded privacy glass that one uses for a bathroom window.

  • Amazon buys rare books to destructively scan them for AI training (\(\mathbb{M}\)).

  • An abbreviation of abbreviation, misspelling of misspelling, and more of the kind from the depths of Wiktionary.

  • Rotating points on four circles form a polygon of constant length by Jim Propp, inspired by Chuck Hoberman’s “Nested Loops” exhibit at the Museum of Mathematics.

  • A cursed triangle in the Moulton plane.

  • If you’ve been working with tagged pdf files in Adobe Acrobat (\(\mathbb{M}\)), you may have noticed an annoying banner that it displays at the top of the window whenever it opens a tagged pdf file: “This file claims compliance with the PDF/A standard and has been opened read-only to prevent modification”. If this banner were only in the default view of Acrobat it might be more easily ignored, but it has no checkbox to make it go away and remains visible even in presentation mode (like, if you’re trying to present a lecture using a tagged pdf file). The only obvious way to make it go away is to click a button labeled “enable editing”, which you might think you don’t want to do.

    It turns out that you can disable these banners entirely. In the preferences window for Acrobat, go to the “Documents” page and change the setting for “PDF/A View Mode” from “Only for PDF/A documents” to “Never”. I suspect that this also disables the automatic read-only setting for these files but I don’t think that’s a problem.

  • Editorial board of Games and Behavior, the journal of the Game Theory Society, resigns (\(\mathbb{M}\)), after its publisher Elsevier replaces its editor-in-chief without consultation with the board, for “closer alignment with Elsevier strategic priorities”. The link leads me to wonder: where is the involvement of the society itself in these decisions?

  • I created this image over a year ago for my CCCG 2025 talk “Decremental greedy polygons and polyhedra without sharp angles” (\(\mathbb{M}\)), but I don’t think I posted it (or the talk slides) online until now. This is what you get from the following process: start with the infinite set of integer points in the positive quadrant, and then repeatedly clip off the point that makes the sharpest angle on the convex hull. As you do this, at certain points you will reach curves for which the sharpest angle is less sharp than for any earlier curve; those are the ones shown in blue. The yellow quarter-circle is added separately for comparison.

    Research problem 1: I don’t understand why the blue curves are so irregularly spaced nor why some of them appear so visually close to quarter-circles. Explain?

  • Physics papers are written in LaTeX (\(\mathbb{M}\)), video by Angela Collier. I doubt anyone here doesn’t already know all this, but it’s a good explainer of why researchers in mathematics/physics/theoretical computer science/linguistics etc. almost universally prefer LaTeX to Word, how the two differ, and why you can infer that a paper in Word was probably not written by a professional. Also with an entertaining rant about why Word is bad, how it’s getting both worse and more expensive, and why you should not pay for it.

  • Digit Party: Three years of lying about high scores (\(\mathbb{M}\)), and how authors Robert Brignall and Vince Vatter switched to integer linear programming in order to finally compute exact high scores for their online digit-clustering puzzle, digit.party.

  • A set of five 60-sided go-first dice (\(\mathbb{M}\), via), found in 2023 by Paul Meyer through efforts coordinated by Auburn University lecturer Eric Harshbarger. These are five dice, labeled so that no two include the same numbers, with equal probabilities of rolling the highest number in all combinations of up to five dice. More strongly Wikipedia states that these dice are “permutation fair”: each permutation of the rolling players is equally likely. Now their discovery is commemorated by a giant set of these dice installed in the Auburn University STEM + Agricultural Sciences Complex.

  • Tsuidoku (\(\mathbb{M}\)), a sudoku variant in which you must fill in the usual 9x9 sudoku grid with both nine digits and nine colors, and must end up with one of each digit-color combination.

    To me the biggest drawback is that the solved puzzles tend to have a stripy pattern like the patterns visible in the sudoku grids packed with 3x3 Latin squares from my recent blog post (both in their colors and digits) and when you detect this pattern it makes the puzzle much easier to solve. Also I’m not a fan of the style of gameplay that announces your mistakes immediately and lets you correct them; I think it makes puzzles trickier (and therefore more interesting) when you have to figure out that you’ve made a mistake yourself and undo back to where you made it. I checked that the nine colors appear distinguishable under the most common form of color blindness (at least to my normal vision eyes using a simulator) but their color contrast was not great, and there are three pairs of indistinguishable colors under blue-blind color blindness (tritanopia).

    All that said, I think the higher levels are tricky enough to be interesting. And (research problem 2) I am intrigued by the question of whether the stripiness is an implementation flaw or a necessary emergent feature of these game rules at this board size.

  • Video on the motion and rigidity of hyperboloids made from sticks (\(\mathbb{M}\)), by Sabetta Matsumoto, Tim Reinhardt, Jürgen Richter-Gebert, and Henry Segerman, in part centered on a large public artwork with this form, Mae West in Munich.

  • Hyperchoreography (\(\mathbb{M}\)), solutions for \(n\)-body problems in more than three dimensions.
